bp: This record is about the Web as a living historical object, not a frozen collection of pages. Pages appear, change, disappear, get archived, are linked from other places, and are later searched by people who care about when something was true. TempWeb serves the community that studies that changing Web. The abstract describes the workshop as a hub for researchers and practitioners who work on infrastructure, scalable methods, and software for aggregating, querying, and analyzing heterogeneous Web data at large scale. The need is practical: a search engine, archive, safety system, or social science study can give the wrong answer if it ignores time. A page about a policy, crisis, product, or person may mean one thing in 2020 and another in 2026. TempWeb's role is to connect the pieces needed to study those changes, from Web archiving and Web mining to temporal information extraction, temporal retrieval, benchmarks, Web evolution, and suicide risk prediction.
wh: The hard part is that the temporal Web is not one neat table. It is many kinds of evidence moving at once: pages, links, timestamps, archived snapshots, user posts, search needs, benchmark tasks, and large infrastructure logs. Some evidence is missing because archives do not capture every page at every moment. Some evidence is inconsistent because different sites record time differently. Some evidence is too large to inspect directly because Web-scale collections require methods that save time, memory, and human effort. The meaning of a query also changes when time enters. Asking for information about an event may mean documents before it, documents after it, documents that changed during it, or documents whose language foreshadowed it. The abstract names a broad spectrum, from Web evolution to suicide risk prediction, which shows the central tension: the field needs shared temporal ways of thinking, but the applications have very different data shapes, risks, and evaluation needs.
naive: A smart beginner might take the normal Web toolkit and add a date filter. Archive pages, store timestamps, run ordinary search, and group papers under whatever application label they mention. That helps only at the surface. It fails because time is not just an extra column. A page can be absent from an archive even though it existed. A query may need the order of changes, not just one date. A prediction task such as suicide risk depends on a trajectory, not one post. A benchmark must define what is observed, what future is hidden, and how systems are compared. The naive approach treats temporal Web analytics as static Web analytics plus calendar labels, so it misses the deeper problem of how evidence changes and how methods should respect that change.
ap: The core idea of this workshop record is coordination around the temporal dimension of the Web. TempWeb is not presented as a single algorithm. It is presented as a recurring research hub that gathers work on the pieces needed to make time a first-class part of Web analysis. In concrete terms, that means bringing together infrastructure for storing and accessing changing Web data, scalable methods for handling large and mixed collections, software for aggregation and querying, and application studies where time changes the answer. The abstract names temporal information extraction and retrieval, Web mining, Web archiving, large-scale data analysis, temporal benchmarks, Web evolution, and suicide risk prediction. The central move is therefore organizational and conceptual: make researchers who might otherwise work separately on archives, search, mining, benchmarks, and health prediction treat their problems as siblings. They are all asking how to recover useful structure from Web evidence whose meaning depends on time.
mech: The mechanism, as far as the abstract supports, is a workshop pipeline rather than a model pipeline. The input is a collection of research contributions from academia and industry, spread across core computer science and application scenarios. Each contribution studies some part of the temporal Web: how to collect heterogeneous Web data, how to aggregate it, how to query it, how to analyze it at scale, how to retrieve information with time in mind, how to extract time-related facts from text, how to build or use Web archives, how to design temporal benchmarks, or how to predict an evolving risk signal. TempWeb then acts as the meeting layer. It places these contributions in one venue, so methods built for infrastructure can be seen next to methods built for retrieval, and application problems can reveal where the underlying tools are still weak. The transformation is not a numerical transformation performed by the paper itself. It is a field-level transformation: separate temporal problems are organized into a shared agenda. The output is a connected research conversation and a clearer map of what temporal Web analytics must support. The abstract explicitly says the 16th edition covers the full spectrum from Web evolution through temporal benchmarks to suicide risk prediction, so the mechanism is broad coverage plus repeated community connection.
math: The main mathematical idea underneath this record is sequence: the order of observations matters. A Web page snapshot, a user post, or a transaction-like event is not only a fact; it is a fact at a particular moment in a longer path. Sequence reasoning asks what happened before, what changed after, and which gaps make the story uncertain. A second idea is retrieval as choosing a small useful set from a huge pile. Temporal retrieval must decide not only which documents match a need, but which versions or time windows match it. A third idea is information extraction, which means turning text into structured clues such as events, dates, and relations so they can be compared or queried. A fourth idea is systems budgeting: Web-scale analysis must save time, memory, and computation because the raw collection is too large for exhaustive inspection. Finally, prediction under uncertainty appears in the suicide risk example and in neighboring temporal benchmark work in the repo. It asks how repeated earlier signals change belief about later states. The tradeoff running through all of this is completeness versus practicality: keeping every temporal detail would be ideal but often impossible, while compressing time too aggressively destroys the evidence that makes the problem temporal.
dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's information retrieval and search family because temporal retrieval is still a ranking problem: from many possible documents or snapshots, the system must return the few that answer a time-sensitive need. It connects to time-series and spatiotemporal work because the Web is treated as a stream of changing observations, not a static store. Neighboring records make that concrete: the FinSurvival Challenge turns time-stamped Web3 events into survival prediction tasks, ANN-TS detects unusual points in high-dimensional Web streams, and the suicide risk paper models a person's online state as a trajectory influenced by posts and comments. TempWeb sits above those examples as connective tissue. It also touches infrastructure and scalability, because archives, benchmarks, and Web-scale analysis cannot succeed if storage and querying are too slow. The broader field-level point is that retrieval, mining, prediction, and archiving all become different faces of the same question once time changes the meaning of evidence.
ww: This works as a research agenda because temporal problems often fail at the boundaries between subfields. An archive can preserve pages but still be hard to query by time. A retrieval method can rank documents but ignore that the same page has several historical versions. A prediction method can use posts but miss how social feedback changes across weeks. A benchmark can compare systems but hide the real temporal difficulties if it ignores missing futures or changing behavior. By gathering these strands, TempWeb increases the chance that a method built in one area exposes assumptions useful to another. Infrastructure work tells application researchers what can actually be collected and queried. Application work tells infrastructure researchers which temporal details matter. Benchmarks force vague progress claims into shared tasks. The abstract's hub language is therefore not just decoration; it describes the practical reason the workshop matters. Time-aware Web research needs repeated contact among people studying data collection, search, mining, scale, and domain-specific consequences.
po: The payoff is a clearer home for temporal Web analytics at The Web Conference. According to the abstract, the 2026 TempWeb edition connects researchers and practitioners across domains and covers infrastructure, scalable methods, innovative software, temporal information extraction and retrieval, Web mining, Web archiving, large-scale analysis, Web evolution, temporal benchmarks, and suicide risk prediction. For the site's reader, the useful capability is conceptual: TempWeb marks these topics as parts of one shared problem rather than scattered specialties. It helps explain why a benchmark paper, an archive paper, a retrieval paper, and a health-risk prediction paper can belong to the same temporal Web conversation.
limits: The abstract is a workshop overview, so it does not prove that one specific method improves accuracy, speed, or reliability. It names areas covered by TempWeb but gives no detailed paper list, experimental setup, benchmark definition, or measured outcome for the workshop itself. The claim that TempWeb is a hub depends on continued participation from researchers and practitioners across the named domains. The technical success of any contribution still depends on its own data quality, time stamps, archive coverage, query design, and evaluation. The abstract supports broad connections across temporal Web topics, but not strong claims about which particular method is best.
